newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania, hit by protest, bans pyramid schemes.
newsitem.headline: Albania, hit by protest, bans pyramid schemes.

text.p: Albania's parliament on Thursday passed a law banning pyramid investment schemes and warned operators they could face a minimum of 20 years in jail and confiscation of their assets.

President Sali Berisha's ruling right-wing Democratic Party quickly pushed the law through parliament in an effort to quell growing protests from investors who stand to lose their life savings in the crumbling investment schemes.
Albanians, some left penniless after the collapse of some of the dubious investment funds, protested in the Adriatic port of Durres and in the northern city of Shkoder on Thursday.
The protests passed peacefully with no reports of violence.

The vote in parliament was passed by 93 votes in favour, with none against. The ruling Democratic Party occupies most seats in the 140-seat assembly as the main opposition parties boycotted disputed general elections last May.
Another draft law concerning compensation for the thousands of investors who have lost money will be considered in a special session on Monday, deputies said.
One member of the ruling Democrats called for the resignation of Finance Minister Ridvan Bode and the head of the state audit commission Blerim Cela over the financial scandal.

But Cela dismissed the criticism, telling deputies: "If the government had passed this law one or two years ago when the pyramid schemes had just started...then it would have been accused of being dictatorial."
Rightist National Front Party chief Hysen Selfo repeated a call from his party for the whole government to resign.
The financial scandals have stirred up the opposition to try to make political capital out of the anger among investors against the Democrats.
The prohibition of the pyramid schemes, which have proliferated since the fall of communism in 1990, was relatively easy for the government to bring about.
But compensating thousands of investors who have poured millions of dollars into the schemes will not be easy for a government struggling to cut a big budget deficit.
Albania's central bank figures put the budget deficit last November at 26.1 billion leks (around $260 million), the equivalent of about 11 percent of gross domestic product.
Authorities have seized around 25.5 billion leks ($255 million) deposited by two collapsed schemes in state-owned banks but the figure may not be enough to quell the anger of Albanians who face ruin.

Around 2,000 demonstrators, accompanied by senior members of the opposition Socialist Party, attempted to converge on the main square of Durres, 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana, but were stopped by police, witnesses said.
"You have to understand us because we are of the people like you, but we have our orders," one police officer was heard telling the protesters.
Protests have spread as investors in Europe's poorest nation face losing their life savings, some after selling their homes, flocks of sheep and cows and other belongings.
Thousands clashed with baton-wielding police in Tirana on Sunday in a demonstration against the schemes, the biggest of several protests around Albania over the past two weeks.
More than 50 people were jailed or fined for taking part in Sunday's protest, described by the authorities as an illegal demonstration.
